stemBlocks.value: A straight line cuts the x-axis at (−3, 0) and the y-axis at (0, 6). (a) Using the formula m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), determine the gradient of the line. (b) Hence write the equation of the line in the form y = mx + c.
Think first: You already have the y-intercept in front of you, so once the gradient is found the equation is complete.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p069-q06 from workbook page 69.

solutionSteps.instruction: Identify c from the y-axis crossing.

contentBlocks.value: The line cuts the y-axis at (0, 6)
y = mx + c with m = 2 and c = 6

strategyBlocks.value: Apply the gradient formula to the two given points, then read c straight from the y-axis crossing and assemble y = mx + c.

whyThisWorks.value: The gradient measures how much y changes for each unit change in x, which is exactly what the difference of the y values divided by the difference of the x values computes. In y = mx + c, c is the value of y when x = 0, so the point where the line meets the y-axis hands you c directly. Subtracting a negative x value is what produces the +3 in the denominator, so the sign work must be done carefully.

commonErrors.misconception: Mixing up the order and computing (x₂ − x₁)/(y₂ − y₁).
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Mixing up the order and computing (x₂ − x₁)/(y₂ − y₁).

commonErrors.misconception: Getting 6/(0 − 3) = −2 by dropping the negative sign on −3.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Getting 6/(0 − 3) = −2 by dropping the negative sign on −3.

commonErrors.misconception: Using −3 as the value of c because it is the x-intercept.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Using −3 as the value of c because it is the x-intercept.

examTip.value: Write the subtraction of a negative in brackets, 0 − (−3), before simplifying; that single habit removes most gradient sign errors.
